lessons.title: Present tense — regular verbs
lessons.summary: Six little endings glued onto the stem — and one present tense that covers both "I work" and "I am working".
lessons.rule:
A verb is the word that says what is happening: wohnen (to live), spielen (to play), lernen (to learn). The form you find in a dictionary is called the infinitive, and in German it nearly always ends in -en.

Cut that -en off and what is left is the stem: wohnen → wohn-, spielen → spiel-. Now you glue a small ending onto the stem, and the ending tells you who is doing it — me, you, him, us. Turkish does exactly the same thing (çalış-ıyor-um); German just has fewer and shorter endings, and there are only six to learn.

If the stem already ends in -t or -d, slide an extra -e in so the word is still sayable: arbeiten → du arbeitest, er arbeitet, ihr arbeitet. Say arbeitst out loud once and you will understand why. Also notice that er wohnt and ihr wohnt look identical — you tell them apart from the word in front, not from the ending.

German has only one present tense. English splits I work and I am working into two different forms. German does not: Ich arbeite is both of them. There is no -ing form at all, so never build something like Ich bin arbeiten — that sentence simply does not exist in German.

The same present tense also does the job of the future. Add a time word and you are finished: Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin means I'm going to Berlin tomorrow. Germans say it this way far more often than with the longer werden-future.

tables.title: Three regular verbs side by side
When the stem ends in -t or -d: an extra -e

examples.note: Stem wohn- plus -e for ich. This is also how you say "I am living in Berlin" — same sentence, no second form.
du takes -st. English needs "are ... doing"; German gets there with one word.
er / sie / es always takes -t on the stem spiel-.
The wir form is identical to the dictionary form lernen. That is not a coincidence — both end in -en.

examples.de: Meine Frau arbeitet in einem Büro.
examples.en: My wife works in an office.
examples.note: "Meine Frau" is a she, so it behaves like er / sie / es. Stem arbeit- ends in -t, so we get -et.
Present tense doing future work. The word morgen (tomorrow) carries the time; the verb stays in the present.

mistakes.why: There is no "am ...-ing" construction in German. Copying English word for word produces a sentence Germans cannot parse — one verb with one ending is the whole thing.
The bare -en form is only for wir and sie/Sie. For er / sie / es you must swap it for -t.
The stem arbeit- already ends in -t, so an -e goes in before the ending. Same for warten, antworten, finden.
Polite Sie is not the du form dressed up — it always takes the -en ending, exactly like sie (they). You will use this every single day at work and in offices.

drills.question: Ich ___ in Berlin.
drills.explain: ich always takes -e, no matter which verb it is.

drills.question: Er ___ jeden Tag Fußball.
drills.explain: er / sie / es takes -t; the -en form would be wir or sie.

drills.question: Du ___ sehr schnell Deutsch. (lernen)
drills.explain: du is the only person that gets the -st ending.

drills.question: "I am living in Hamburg" in German is:
drills.explain: German has no continuous form, so the plain present has to cover the English -ing meaning too.

drills.question: Wir ___ um acht Uhr. (kommen)
drills.explain: wir keeps the -en, which makes it look like the dictionary form.

drills.question: Ihr ___ zu viel. (arbeiten)
drills.explain: ihr normally takes -t, but a stem ending in -t needs a linking -e first or nobody could pronounce it.
A present-tense verb plus a future time word is the normal way Germans talk about tomorrow.
"Meine Tochter" counts as she, so the verb takes the er / sie / es ending -t.

lessons.title: Stem-changing verbs — fahren, nehmen, lesen
lessons.summary: A handful of everyday verbs change their vowel — but only in the du and er/sie/es forms, nowhere else.
lessons.rule:
Some of the most common German verbs quietly change the vowel inside their stem (the part left after you remove -en). The endings stay exactly the ones you already know. Only the vowel moves.

And it happens in only two places: the du form and the er / sie / es form. ich, wir, ihr and sie / Sie are completely normal. If you remember nothing else, remember that: two forms, then back to normal.

There are three changes. a → ä: fahren (to drive/go) gives du fährst, er fährt. e → i: nehmen (to take) gives du nimmst, er nimmt. e → ie: lesen (to read) gives du liest, er liest.

Two of them need a small warning. nehmen loses its h and doubles the m — it is nimmt, not nihmt. And with lesen the stem lies- already ends in an s-sound, so the -st ending gives up its s: du liest, not du liesst. That means du and er look identical here. Same thing with essen: du isst, er isst.

There is no rule that tells you in advance which verbs do this — you learn them one at a time. The consolation is that it is a short list, and they are verbs you will say twenty times a day: fahren, nehmen, lesen, sprechen, geben, essen, schlafen, tragen, laufen, sehen.

tables.title: More of them you will meet every day

examples.de: Ich fahre mit dem Bus, aber Anna fährt mit dem Rad.
examples.en: I go by bus, but Anna goes by bike.
examples.note: Same verb, same sentence: ich stays plain fahre, Anna counts as she and gets the umlaut — fährt.
nehmen → nimmst. The h disappears and the m doubles. You will hear this one in every German kitchen.

examples.de: Er liest jeden Abend die Zeitung.
examples.en: He reads the newspaper every evening.
examples.note: lesen → liest. The e stretches into ie.
sprechen → sprichst, e becomes i. Compare: ich spreche, wir sprechen — untouched.
Proof that wir keeps the plain stem. The change never leaves du and er / sie / es.
geben → gibt for er / sie / es.

mistakes.why: Once you learn nimmst / nimmt it is tempting to use that stem everywhere. The ich form never changes — it stays nehme.
The umlaut is not decoration; du fahrst is simply not a German word. a → ä in du and er / sie / es.
The opposite error: spreading the umlaut to wir. Only two persons change, and wir is not one of them.
The stem already ends in an s-sound, so the -st ending drops its s. Same with du isst (essen) and du heißt (heißen).

drills.question: Du ___ morgen nach Hamburg.
drills.explain: du triggers the a → ä change; fahrt without umlaut is the ihr form.

drills.question: Er ___ immer den Bus.
drills.explain: er / sie / es turns nehm- into nimm-, and the -t ending goes on top.

drills.question: Wir ___ am Wochenende nach Köln. (fahren)
drills.explain: wir is outside the two changing forms, so the vowel stays untouched.

drills.question: ___ du Deutsch?
drills.explain: sprechen changes e → i for du, and Spricht would be the er / sie / es form.

drills.question: Du ___ jeden Tag die Zeitung. (lesen)
drills.explain: The stem becomes lies-, and because it ends in an s-sound the ending loses its own s.

drills.question: Ihr ___ zu schnell. (sprechen)
drills.explain: ihr is a normal form — plain stem plus -t, no vowel change at all.
geben becomes gibt for er, and the verb sits in second position as usual.

drills.answer: Nimmst du den Bus oder das Auto
drills.explain: A yes/no question starts with the verb — and the du form still carries the i, so it is Nimmst, not Nehmst.

lessons.title: sein, haben, werden — the three you cannot avoid
lessons.summary: To be, to have, to become: wildly irregular, in every second sentence, and the machinery behind the past tense and the passive.
lessons.rule:
sein means to be, haben means to have, werden means to become or to get. You will use all three in your first conversation in Germany and in every one after that.

They are irregular in a way no other verbs are. Look at sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist. Not one of those looks like sein. There is nothing to work out here — these are the tables you simply memorise, and they buy you more than any other page in this course.

The tables below also give the Präteritum. That is just the grammar name for the simple past: I was, I had, it became. For most German verbs you will use a different past form in conversation, but for these three the Präteritum is what people actually say: war, hatte, wurde. "Ich war gestern krank" is normal spoken German.

These three are also helper verbs (grammar books say auxiliary) — a verb that adds no meaning of its own and just holds a bigger structure together. haben and sein build the everyday past: Ich habe gegessen (I ate), Ich bin gefahren (I went). werden builds the future and the passive — the passive is when you say what happens to something without naming who does it: Das Auto wird repariert = the car is being repaired. You do not need those yet, but every one of them runs on this page.

Finally, watch where German picks a different verb than English. Hunger, thirst and fear are things you have: Ich habe Hunger, literally "I have hunger". Your age is something you are: Ich bin 30 Jahre alt. And being cold is neither — Germans say Mir ist kalt, literally "to me it is cold". Ich bin kalt says something about your personality.

tables.title: Where German picks the other verb

examples.note: sein for jobs — and German drops the article: not "ein Ingenieur".
haben loses its b in du and er / sie / es: du hast, er hat.

examples.de: Ich habe Hunger. Gehen wir essen?
examples.en: I'm hungry. Shall we go eat?
examples.note: German owns its hunger. "Ich bin Hunger" sounds like you are claiming to be a feeling.
war is the simple past of sein and is used constantly in speech — much more than the longer past form.
werden = to become / to get. Es ist kalt would mean it already is cold.

examples.de: Wir hatten letzte Woche kein Internet.
examples.en: We had no internet last week.
examples.note: hatten — the wir form of the simple past of haben.

mistakes.why: English says "I am hungry", so the hand writes bin automatically. German treats hunger, thirst and fear as things you possess, so they take haben.
Ich bin kalt describes you as a cold person. To say your body feels cold, German puts the cold outside you: mir ist kalt, "to me it is cold".
The er / sie / es form of werden is a short irregular word, wird. You do not add -t to it, and du is wirst, not werdst.

mistakes.wrong: Ich habe gestern in Köln gewesen.
mistakes.why: Two errors at once: sein never builds its past with haben, and in normal speech you would use war anyway rather than any longer form.

drills.question: Ich ___ aus der Türkei.
drills.explain: sein has a separate, unrelated word for each person — ich gets bin and nothing else.

drills.question: ___ du heute Zeit?
drills.explain: haben drops its b in the du and er forms, so the regular-looking Habst does not exist.

drills.question: Wir ___ um acht zu Hause. (sein)
drills.explain: wir and sie / Sie share the same form of sein, sind.

drills.question: Ich ___ Hunger.
drills.explain: German counts hunger as something you own rather than something you are.

drills.question: Es ___ langsam kalt. (werden)
drills.explain: werden describes a change in progress — the weather is turning cold, not simply being cold.

drills.question: Gestern ___ ich krank. (sein — Präteritum)
drills.explain: For sein the simple past is what Germans really say; the longer past form sounds heavy in conversation.
hatten is the wir form of the simple past of haben, and the verb keeps its second-position seat.
Turning an age is a change of state, so German uses werden here where English would use "is".
